meta.blurb: At 7:42 every morning the train stops for a minute beside a garden, and a woman in a yellow coat waves. Then one day she hangs washing with the wrong hand and does not wave. Only Mina, a secretly jobless bookkeeper, notices.
meta.bible: Mina Hale: a bookkeeper in her thirties who lost her job at the Dunmore Bakery two months ago and has told nobody; she notices small details and keeps a notebook. Hettie: Mina's younger sister. Clara Vane: the woman in the yellow coat at Number 12 Larch Terrace; right-handed, kind, sings in a choir, keeps the Larch Hall Fund account book. Colin Vane: Clara's husband, treasurer of the Larch Hall Fund, owner of Vane Roofing; charming and guilty. Fern Pollard: Colin's sister, left-handed, wears Clara's yellow coat to pretend Clara is at home. Joe Marsh: Clara's older brother, the signal box keeper at Larch Crossing. Tomás Reyes: the cheerful train guard. Priya Bannister: Detective Sergeant at Eastfield police station. Rosa Bell: Clara's friend from the choir. Mr Dobbs: grumpy gossiping neighbour at Number 14. Eastfield: the town and station; Platform Nine is where Mina boards the 7:42 train to Harbour. Harbour: the city with the library. Larch Terrace: the row of houses beside the railway. Larch Crossing: where the train stops at a red signal near the signal box. Yellow Coat: Mina's name for Clara. Larch Hall Fund: money for a new roof for the little hall; about forty thousand pounds raised, about thirty-eight thousand pounds taken. Three payments to Vane Roofing share one invoice number, and one is dated on a Sunday when the bank was closed. Voice and tone: a warm, gently suspenseful mystery for general readers; no violence and no gore; fair-play clues (left hand, no wave, yellow glove on the windowsill, the Sunday payment).

A woman in a yellow coat hung washing and waved at the train.
Mina called her Yellow Coat and waved back every single morning.
Tomás, the train guard, said good morning to Mina every day.
At the library, Mina looked for jobs, but she found nothing.
On Monday, Yellow Coat waved late, and she looked very tired.
On Tuesday, the garden was empty, and a man closed the curtain.
On Wednesday, the garden was empty again, and the wait felt longer.
On Thursday, a woman in the yellow coat hung washing but did not wave.

Mina looked at her photo and knew something was very wrong.
On Saturday, Mina went to the police and told her story.

Rosa said that Clara found some numbers that were wrong.
Mina found the money for the hall roof, but it was gone.

Mr Dobbs, the neighbour, said the woman in yellow was rude.
Mr Dobbs said someone walked the path with a torch.
Colin Vane met Mina at his gate and smiled politely.
Mina saw Fern writing a note with her left hand.
Mina told Tomás her story, and he listened carefully.
Mina wrote down why Fern wore the yellow coat.
A grey car followed Mina to the station.

In her photo, Mina saw a yellow glove on a window.

B1B2: Every weekday, Mina Hale walked onto Platform Nine at Eastfield station and boarded the 7:42 train to Harbour. She always chose the same seat, on the left, beside the window.

Two months earlier, the Dunmore Bakery had closed its office, and Mina had lost her job as a bookkeeper. She had told nobody, so she still took the train every day and spent her hours at the library in Harbour.
Halfway to Harbour, the train always stopped at a red signal at a place called Larch Crossing. The wait lasted about a minute, and nobody on board ever seemed to mind.

Beyond the window lay the back gardens of Larch Terrace, each with a small gate onto the cinder path beside the railway. In the garden of Number 12, a woman in a yellow coat was hanging out washing, and she waved at the train.
Mina had named the woman Yellow Coat, and every morning she waved back. She had noticed that the woman always waved with her right hand and held a warm mug in her left.

Tomás Reyes, the guard, always stopped to say good morning, and today he blamed the red signal on a man called Joe. Joe Marsh had worked in the little signal box at Larch Crossing for twenty years, and he was never late.
At the library in Harbour, Mina sent four job applications before lunch. Then her sister Hettie sent a message asking how work was going, and Mina lied and said it was busy.
On Monday the woman in the yellow coat came out late, and her wave was slow. She kept glancing back at her kitchen window, as if she was afraid of something.
On Tuesday there was no washing on the line and no one at the gate. Only a tall man stood at the kitchen window of Number 12, and he pulled the curtain shut as the train went by.
On Wednesday the garden was empty again, and the train waited at the signal for nearly three minutes. Tomás said that Joe had blamed a fault in a cable, though he looked puzzled when he said it.

On Thursday a woman in the yellow coat hung out the washing, but she kept her back to the train and did not wave. Mina noticed that she pegged the sheets with her left hand, so she took a quick photo on her phone.

On Friday, a newspaper showed a smiling woman in a yellow coat, and her name was Clara Vane. Her friend Rosa Bell said she had been missing since Monday, but her husband Colin said she had gone away to rest.
Mina looked again at the photograph from Thursday, and then at the notes in her notebook. The woman on Thursday had used her left hand and had never waved, so it could not have been the same woman.
On Saturday morning Mina walked into Eastfield police station and asked to speak to someone about Clara Vane. A calm woman called Detective Sergeant Priya Bannister listened carefully to everything.

Sergeant Bannister said that a grown woman is allowed to leave her home, and that a neighbour had seen Mrs Vane on Thursday. She thanked Mina, but she asked her to bring something more solid than a waving hand.
Mina found Rosa Bell at choir practice in the church hall, and Rosa was glad to talk. Clara, she said, was right-handed, never missed a rehearsal, and had been worried about money lately.
Rosa said that Clara had found numbers that did not add up in the Larch Hall Fund. The fund paid for the little hall's new roof, and Clara's husband Colin was its treasurer.
At the library, Mina found the fund's yearly accounts on a notice board website. About forty thousand pounds had been collected for the roof, yet the balance at the bank was only a few thousand.
In the library's old newspapers, Mina found a short story about Vane Roofing. Last spring the company had almost gone bankrupt, owing money to many suppliers, and its owner was Colin Vane.
Mr Dobbs lived at Number 14, and he shouted at the trains every morning. He told Mina that he had seen Clara on Thursday, but that she had not even said good morning, which he thought was very rude.
Mr Dobbs added that somebody had been walking up and down the cinder path at night with a torch. He had not seen a face, but he had heard a car door close in the lane.

Colin Vane was waiting at his front gate when Mina walked past, and his smile was warm and friendly. He said that Clara needed rest and that his sister Fern had been a great help, but his eyes stayed cold.

Later that day, Mina saw a woman in the garden of Number 12, and this time she was close enough to see her face. It was Fern Pollard, Colin's sister, and she wrote a note on the gatepost with her left hand.

On Monday evening Mina told Tomás everything, and he listened without laughing. Then he said, slowly, that Joe Marsh had started leaving two mugs on his signal box windowsill, and that Joe never had visitors.
That night Mina worked out why Fern had worn the coat. If neighbours saw Clara at home, nobody would search for her, and Colin would have time to find whatever he needed.
On Tuesday morning a grey car seemed to follow Mina all the way to the station. She told herself that she was imagining things, but she walked faster just the same.

That afternoon Sergeant Bannister called Mina to say that Colin Vane had complained about a stranger bothering his family. She warned Mina kindly to keep her distance until there was real evidence of a crime.
Hettie visited that evening, and Mina finally told her about the lost job and about Yellow Coat. Her sister was not angry, and she said, “Then use what you are good at.”
Later Mina enlarged the Thursday photograph until the signal box filled her screen. On the windowsill lay a yellow glove, exactly like the ones Clara wore to hang out the washing.
Mina remembered the small gate at the bottom of Clara's garden and the cinder path beside the railway. It led, only a few minutes away, straight to Joe Marsh's signal box.
On Saturday morning Mina walked along the cinder path until she reached the signal box. A big, grey-haired man opened the door, and he said that visitors were not allowed.
Mina told Joe that she was the woman in the window seat of the 7:42, and that she had waved to Clara every morning. For a long moment the big man said nothing at all.
A voice from the stairs said, “Let her in, Joe.” A pale woman in a borrowed cardigan came down, and Mina knew her at once as Clara Vane.
Clara explained that Joe was her brother, and that Marsh was her name before she married. She had come to hide with him because she had found something terrible about the hall fund.
On Monday afternoon Clara had found that about thirty-eight thousand pounds had left the fund. That night she faced Colin, and he begged her to keep quiet.

That night Clara took the account book and the bank papers, slipped through her back gate, and walked the cinder path to Joe's box. She dared not tell the police yet, because she had no proof that anybody would trust.
Each morning Clara watched the 7:42 from the box window, and she had hoped to wave to the lady in the window seat. She had not dared to show herself, because Colin's car might pass at any moment.
Clara studied Mina's photograph of the Thursday woman and sighed. It was Colin's sister Fern, she said, who had always borrowed her clothes and who was left-handed.
Mina asked if she could look at the account book, because numbers were the one thing she knew. Clara hesitated, then pushed the heavy book across the table.
Mina found three payments to Vane Roofing that all carried the same invoice number. One of them was dated on a Sunday, when the bank was closed, so it could not be real.
As Mina left the cinder path, Mr Dobbs looked over his fence and saw her. He was a gossip, and by noon he had told Colin Vane exactly where she had been.
That Sunday Mina called Sergeant Bannister and explained about the invoices and the Sunday payment. Bannister was quiet, and then she said that she would come to the signal box on Monday morning.
That evening Mina and Hettie made a plan for Monday. Mina would ride the 7:42 as usual, so that nobody would suspect anything, and Hettie would wait by her phone.
On Monday morning Mina boarded the 7:42 at Platform Nine and took her usual seat by the window. Tomás gave her a small wink as he walked down the carriage.
Meanwhile, Colin Vane and his sister Fern were hurrying along the cinder path toward the signal box. Fern was wearing the yellow coat again, because Colin wanted any watchers to think it was Clara.
At 7:43 the train slowed and stopped at the red signal, exactly as it did every morning. At the same moment Mina saw Colin Vane step up to the door of the signal box.
Tomás stood in the aisle and spoke clearly to the whole carriage, and every passenger turned to look out of the window. Dozens of phones went up to film Colin Vane as he pounded on the door.
The door of the signal box opened, and Clara Vane stepped out and waved with her right hand. Half the train gasped, because many of them had named her Yellow Coat too.
Sergeant Bannister and a colleague arrived along the path at a quarter to eight, and Colin Vane had nowhere to go. Fern admitted at once that she had worn the coat, and Colin did not say a word.
Colin Vane was charged, and the hall fund was slowly put right, with Mina hired to check the accounts. A week later she took the 7:42 again, and Clara waved at the train from her garden.
C1C2: With the mist still lifting off the car park, Mina Hale climbed aboard the 7:42 at Platform Nine and settled into the window seat on the left, as she had done for years. It was a small habit, but she had learned that small habits can hold a person together when much else has come loose. Outside, the station lamps were fading as the sky turned from grey to pale gold.

The Dunmore Bakery had shut its office in August, and with it went Mina's position as bookkeeper, a post she had held for six dull and comfortable years. She had not been able to tell her family, partly from shame and partly from the stubborn hope that a new job would arrive before the truth had to. So each morning she dressed as usual, boarded the same train, and went to hide among the shelves of the Harbour library.

Halfway to Harbour, where the line bends past a row of tired brick houses, the 7:42 always slowed and came to rest at a red signal beside Larch Crossing. The delay never lasted longer than a minute, and the other commuters used it to sigh, scroll through their phones, or close their eyes. Mina, however, had come to treasure that minute above every other part of her day.

Beyond the glass lay the back gardens of Larch Terrace, with their sagging fences, their sheds, and a narrow gate at the bottom of each plot that opened onto the cinder path beside the railway. In the garden of Number 12 a woman in a bright yellow coat was pegging out sheets, and as the train stood waiting she lifted her hand and waved. Nobody else in the carriage looked up, but Mina felt, absurdly, that she had been noticed.

Over the weeks Mina had christened her Yellow Coat, and the two of them had developed a silent ritual that neither would ever have admitted was a friendship. Being a bookkeeper by training, Mina noticed small details almost without trying, and she had seen that the woman always waved with her right hand while a steaming mug waited in her left. On cold mornings she wore bright yellow gardening gloves, which made her wave look like a small flag.

Tomás Reyes, the guard, was a broad and cheerful man who made a point of greeting every regular passenger by name, and he paused beside Mina's seat with a ticket machine hanging from his shoulder. The red light, he explained with mock solemnity, was the work of Joe Marsh, who had operated the little signal box at Larch Crossing for twenty years and never once been late. Mina smiled, glanced at the box beside the garden wall, and noticed that its windows were small and dusty, like the eyes of a sleepy animal.

In the hush of the Harbour library, Mina sent four careful applications before noon and received, in return, four automatic replies that thanked her for her interest. At lunchtime a message arrived from her younger sister Hettie, who asked how the bakery was treating her and whether she was working too hard. Mina typed that everything was fine and very busy, then sat looking at the words, which felt heavier than any lie she had told before.

On Monday the woman in the yellow coat appeared in her garden later than usual, and she lifted her hand to the train with none of her old brightness. She did not touch the washing basket at her feet, and twice she turned to look back at the kitchen window, like someone listening for a sound. When the signal turned green and the train pulled away, Mina was left with a small, unaccountable chill.

On Tuesday the garden of Number 12 was empty, the washing line hung bare, and the back gate stood closed against the cinder path. A tall man appeared at the kitchen window, looked at the waiting train with an expression Mina could not read, and drew the curtain across as though to shut out the world. She told herself that people have days off from washing, yet her notebook stayed open on her knee for the rest of the journey.

On Wednesday the curtains stayed closed and the garden remained empty, and for some reason the signal held the train for nearly three minutes instead of one. Tomás, wandering down the carriage to calm the grumbling passengers, mentioned that Joe Marsh had blamed a fault in a cable. He said it with a puzzled frown, because in twenty years he had never known Joe to be anything but exact.

On Thursday the yellow coat returned to the garden at last, yet the figure inside it kept her back firmly turned to the train, and she did not wave. Mina watched her peg the sheets with her left hand, awkwardly, as one might use a tool that belonged to someone else, and with a faint prickle of unease she lifted her phone and took a photograph. The picture caught the woman, the washing, and behind them the grimy little signal box and its windowsill.

At the station kiosk on Friday morning, Mina saw the face of Yellow Coat smiling up from the front page of the local newspaper, and the breath went out of her. The article explained that Clara Vane of Larch Terrace had not been seen by her friends since Monday, and that Rosa Bell, a fellow singer in her choir, had raised the alarm. Her husband Colin, however, insisted that Clara had gone away to rest, and a neighbour claimed to have seen her at home on Thursday morning.

On the train Mina laid the Thursday photograph beside the pages of her notebook, where she had recorded, in her careful bookkeeper's hand, every habit of the woman at Number 12. Clara Vane waved with her right hand and she waved every morning without fail, while the person in the garden on Thursday had done neither, and had even pegged the sheets with the wrong hand. If a neighbour had seen Clara at home that morning, then the neighbour had been looking at somebody else.

On Saturday morning Mina walked into Eastfield police station, gave her name at the desk, and asked, with a nervousness she tried to hide, to speak to somebody about Clara Vane. A calm woman in a grey jacket introduced herself as Detective Sergeant Priya Bannister, led her to a small room that smelled of tea, and listened without interrupting. When Mina had finished, the sergeant turned a pen over in her fingers, and the silence stretched out a little too long.

Sergeant Bannister explained, gently but plainly, that a grown woman has every right to leave her home, and that a neighbour had seen Mrs Vane alive and well on Thursday morning. She thanked Mina for the photograph, noted its time and date, and observed that people sometimes change their habits when they are unhappy. Then she added, with a faint smile, that if Mina could bring her something more solid than a missing wave, she would be glad to look again.

Mina found Rosa Bell at the church hall where the choir met, and the older woman seized on her story as if it were a lifeline. Clara, Rosa declared, was right-handed and as punctual as a church clock, and in all the years she had sung with them she had never once missed a rehearsal without telling someone. Something had been troubling her lately, she added, something to do with money, and Clara had not wished to say more.

Rosa lowered her voice and confided that, only a week earlier, Clara had mentioned some numbers in the Larch Hall Fund that did not add up. The fund had been collected over several years from the residents to pay for a new roof on the little hall, and Clara's husband Colin was its treasurer, while Clara herself kept the account book. Rosa did not like to suspect anyone, she said, but a woman who vanishes without a word to her friends is a woman with something on her mind.

At the Harbour library on Monday, Mina searched the residents' website and found the hall fund's yearly summary, a document that her professional eye could not help but read as a story. About forty thousand pounds had been gathered for the new roof, yet the bank balance printed on the last page was only a few thousand, and the difference was explained by a single line reading, repairs and works. A bookkeeper learns that when a large sum hides behind a vague phrase, the phrase is usually where to look.

Searching the library's archive of the local newspaper, Mina came upon a short paragraph that made her sit up straight in her chair. Vane Roofing, it reported, had nearly collapsed the previous spring under the weight of debts to its suppliers, and its owner, Colin Vane, had begged for more time. If a man's own business was drowning in the spring and a community fund sat in his keeping, then the question of where the roof money went suddenly had a very plain shape.

Mr Dobbs of Number 14 was a bristling old man who shook his fist at the passing trains every morning, and Mina approached him with some caution over the fence. He was perfectly certain that he had seen Clara Vane on Thursday, because he had recognised the famous yellow coat, but she had walked straight past him without a word of greeting. In forty years of living beside her, he grumbled, she had never been so rude.

Before Mina could escape his fence, Mr Dobbs added that someone had been prowling the cinder path behind the houses after dark, sweeping a torch over the sheds and the signal box. He had not seen a face, he said, but he had heard a car door slam in the lane at midnight and a man muttering to himself. It was the kind of detail that people mention only because it troubles them, and it troubled Mina too.

As Mina passed Number 12 on the street side, the front door opened and Colin Vane stepped out, a tall man in a neat cardigan whose smile seemed generous and entirely rehearsed. He said that he had heard she was asking questions, that Clara had simply needed a rest, and that his sister Fern had been a tower of strength all week. Mina nodded politely, but she noticed that while his mouth was smiling his eyes were counting her, as though she were a column of figures that might not add up.

A little later Mina saw the yellow coat again, hanging on the line at Number 12, and its owner stood nearby with a pen, writing a label with her left hand. From the lane at the end of the garden she could see that the woman was older than Clara, with dyed hair and a sharper chin, and a neighbour's greeting soon gave her name as Fern Pollard. Fern was Colin's sister, and she had been borrowing her sister-in-law's coat to play her part.

On the train home Mina told Tomás everything, from the stranger in the yellow coat to the money missing from the hall fund, and to her surprise he did not laugh. He scratched his chin and said, after a long moment, that Joe Marsh had lately begun leaving two mugs on the signal box windowsill, and Joe was a man who had never had a visitor in twenty years. It was a very small clue, but it made both of them look out of the window at the little box in the dusk.

That night, at her kitchen table, Mina set out the problem the way she would have reconciled an account, and the answer came with a satisfying click. Fern had worn the coat to persuade the neighbourhood that Clara was home and safe, because a woman who has been seen alive will not be searched for. Every hour that nobody searched gave Colin another hour to find whatever he was looking for, and the only question left was where the real Clara had gone.

On Tuesday morning a grey car followed Mina along the road to the station, keeping a polite distance, and it was parked outside the library when she came out at lunchtime. She told herself that Eastfield was full of grey cars and that her imagination had been feeding on too much worry, yet her steps quickened all the same. It is one thing to wonder about a stranger's secrets, and quite another to discover that the stranger is wondering about yours.

That afternoon Sergeant Bannister telephoned to say, with obvious reluctance, that Colin Vane had lodged a complaint about a stranger who was bothering his family and asking questions in the street. She advised Mina, in the tone of someone who would rather have said something different, to keep her distance until there was real evidence of a crime. Mina thanked her politely, put the phone away, and understood that the only person now standing between Colin Vane and his secret was a jobless bookkeeper.

Hettie arrived that evening unannounced, with a bag of oranges and a worried expression, and the whole story came tumbling out of Mina at last, from the lost job to the woman in the yellow coat. Her sister did not scold or gasp but simply held her hand, as she had done when they were children, and said that a bookkeeper who could not find missing money was no bookkeeper at all. It was the first time in weeks that Mina felt the knot in her chest begin to loosen.

Late that night Mina enlarged Thursday's photograph, pinching the screen until the little signal box swelled to fill it, and then she held her breath. On the dusty windowsill lay a single yellow glove, drying in the pale light, the very twin of the pair Clara had worn on cold mornings to peg out the sheets. The woman who had vanished had not gone to Wales, and she had not gone far.

Everything now connected: the narrow gate at the bottom of Clara's garden, the cinder path that ran beside the railway, and, only a few minutes' walk along it, the little box where Joe Marsh had set out two mugs. A woman who needed to disappear from her own house, quietly and in the dark, could not have chosen a better road. Mina closed her notebook, lay awake for hours, and resolved to walk that path on Saturday.

On Saturday morning, with the mist still clinging to the rails, Mina walked the length of the cinder path until the signal box rose in front of her, small and square and smelling of coal smoke. A heavy, grey-haired man opened the door before she could knock, folded his arms across his chest, and informed her that visitors were strictly forbidden. His eyes, however, kept flickering nervously toward the narrow wooden stairs behind him, as though someone were listening there.

Mina stood her ground and explained that she was the woman in the window seat of the 7:42, the one who had waved to Clara every morning for months. She said that she was not from the police, and that Colin Vane did not know she was there, but that she had a feeling that someone in the signal box needed a friend. The big man's jaw tightened, and the silence between them grew so long that she could hear a kettle ticking somewhere inside.

Then a voice from the stairs said quietly, “Let her in, Joe,” and a pale, tired woman in a borrowed cardigan came slowly down into the light. Mina knew her at once, though she had only ever seen her from a train window, and in her relief she almost laughed aloud. Clara Vane was safe, and she had been alive and warm within sight of that window for days.

Over mugs of strong tea Clara explained that Joe was her older brother, that Marsh was her name before she married, and that she had come to him in the dark because he was the one person she trusted completely. She had been checking the hall fund's bank statements, she said, partly from habit and partly from a small voice of doubt, and what she had found had made her feel quite ill. Then, with a shaky laugh, she added that she had never thought a stranger on a train would find her.

On Monday afternoon, Clara said, the truth had arrived like a bucket of cold water: about thirty-eight thousand pounds had left the hall fund in small payments, each one signed off in her husband's neat handwriting. That evening she had faced him in the kitchen, and Colin, after the first denials, had wept and begged her to give him time to put it right. She had looked at him and realised that, for the first time in twenty years, she did not believe a word he said.

Clara waited until Colin had gone upstairs, then took the account book and the bank papers, tucked them under her arm, and slipped out of the back gate onto the cinder path. She had walked to the signal box in the dark with a pounding heart, knowing that she could not yet go to the police, because Colin was liked by everyone and she had only her own word against his. Her brother, without asking a single question, had opened the door and put the kettle on.

Each morning, Clara admitted, she had stood back from the box window and watched the 7:42 draw up beneath her, searching the carriages for the woman in the window seat. She had wanted desperately to wave, but she had not dared to show herself in case Colin's car passed on the lane behind. It had been, she said with a rueful smile, the loneliest week of her life, and the only part of her old routine that she missed.

Clara studied Mina's photograph of the Thursday woman for a long moment and then sighed with something between anger and sadness. That was Fern, she said, her husband's sister, who had been borrowing her clothes for years and who was as left-handed as a person could be. It would be just like Fern, she added, to wear the yellow coat and keep her face turned away so no one would know.

Mina asked, with a bookkeeper's polite urgency, whether she might look through the account book, since numbers were the one language in which she had always been fluent. Clara hesitated for only a moment before pushing the heavy volume across the little table, and Joe fetched a lamp so that they could all see. For the first time in two months, Mina felt entirely and wonderfully useful, as if a long-locked door had finally swung open.

Within half an hour Mina had found what the police would need, because three large payments to Vane Roofing all carried the same invoice number, a mistake that no honest company would make. One of the entries was dated on a Sunday, when the fund's bank was closed to everybody, and the handwriting in that line was a little different from the rest, as though written in a hurry. Clara looked at the page and whispered that it was exactly what she had been afraid to see.

As Mina walked back along the cinder path at the end of the afternoon, a pair of suspicious eyes followed her from the fence of Number 14. Mr Dobbs was a notorious gossip who liked to be first with the news, and by evening he had mentioned to Colin Vane, over the garden wall, that the woman asking questions had been seen walking toward the signal box. Mina knew nothing of it, but the walls around Clara were already beginning to close.

On Sunday morning Mina telephoned Sergeant Bannister and laid out the whole matter: the repeated invoice number, the payment dated on a day the bank was shut, and the woman who had not gone to Wales. There was a long pause on the line, and then the sergeant said, in a changed voice, that she would meet them at the signal box at a quarter to eight on Monday. Nobody, she added, should touch the account book until she arrived, and for the first time in a week Mina felt that the law was on her side.

That evening Mina sat up with Hettie at the kitchen table and settled the plan for Monday morning, going over it twice like an examination. She would ride the 7:42 exactly as she had on every other weekday, so that Colin would suspect nothing, and Tomás would keep an eye out from the guard's van. Hettie, who was more nervous than she admitted, promised to stay beside her phone until the whole thing was over.

On Monday morning the platform was cold and the sky was the colour of pewter, and Mina climbed aboard the 7:42 with a heart that thudded like a drum. She took her familiar seat beside the window, pressed her hand to her notebook for courage, and was grateful when Tomás passed down the aisle and gave her a small, deliberate wink. Whatever happened at Larch Crossing that morning, she knew at least that she would not be facing it entirely alone.

Meanwhile, along the cinder path from the lane, Colin Vane and his sister were making their way toward the signal box with the grim haste of people who have run out of time. Fern wore the yellow coat once more, since Colin had worked out that the sight of it would calm any curious neighbour, and he carried a heavy bag in which he meant to put the account book. They did not look at the sky, or at the line, or at the time.

At 7:43 the train slowed and came to rest at its usual red signal, and this time the stop was no accident, since Joe Marsh had been given a plan and a reason. Mina pressed her forehead to the glass and saw Colin Vane, three carriages' length away, put his hand on the door of the signal box and begin to hammer on it. She seized her phone, sent a single word to Tomás, and watched the guard step quickly toward the front of the train.

Tomás stood in the middle of the carriage and announced, in his warmest and most carrying voice, that anyone who wished could watch a rather interesting scene at the signal box. In an instant every commuter turned to the windows, laptops closed and phones rose, and dozens of eyes and cameras fixed upon the tall man hammering at the door. It was, in all the years that Mina had ridden it, the first time that the 7:42 had ever fallen completely and utterly silent.

Then the door swung open and Clara Vane stepped out into the morning light, without her coat, and lifted her right hand to the train in the old familiar wave. A gasp ran through the carriages, followed by a ripple of cheers, because Mina discovered in that moment that half the commuters on the 7:42 had known the woman in the garden and had loved her silently for years. Beside her, Fern Pollard stood frozen in the yellow coat, and Colin's face had turned the colour of paper.

Sergeant Bannister and a young constable came striding along the path at a quarter to eight, and Colin Vane, watched by a hundred witnesses, saw every road of escape close behind him. Fern burst into tears and admitted that she had worn the yellow coat on her brother's orders, and Colin, for the first time, did not have a smooth word to offer. Clara handed the account book to the sergeant with a hand that no longer shook.

Colin Vane was charged with fraud that same week, and in time most of the hall fund's money was recovered, while the trustees, impressed by a bookkeeper who could read a Sunday payment, hired Mina to audit their accounts. She told Hettie, and her mother, and Tomás the whole truth, and none of them minded about the lost job at all. The next Monday she rode the 7:42 with a real reason to be on it, and when it stopped at the red signal, a woman in a yellow coat was waving from the garden of Number 12.
